analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue employers who pay women less and harder for them to justify it.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 221 House cosponsors, including 220 of the chamber's Democrats, but never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthens the Equal Pay Act so an employer can only justify paying a woman less than a man with a job-related, business-necessity reason that explains the whole gap. It bans employers from asking a job applicant's salary history, protects workers who discuss their wages from retaliation, adds compensatory and punitive damages for victims, and requires large employers to report pay data by sex, race, and national origin so discrimination can be detected.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and workers in protected classes who are underpaid relative to coworkers doing the same work. The bill gives them stronger lawsuits, broader damages including attorney and expert fees, class-action rights, and an easier path because employers must prove their pay gap reason is job-related. It also bans employers from using a new hire's prior salary to justify a lower starting wage, which stops past discrimination from following workers from job to job.

how_it_helps.text: An employer claiming a pay gap is based on education, training, or experience must prove the factor is job-related, consistent with business necessity, and accounts for the entire differential, and loses the defense if a less discriminatory alternative would serve the same business purpose [S3].
Employees win compensatory damages, punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, and expert fees; equal pay claims can proceed as class actions [S3].

Employers may not seek or rely on a prospective employee's wage history in hiring or pay decisions, with civil penalties of $5,000 per first violation and up to $10,000 in special damages per affected worker [S3].

The bill makes it unlawful to require employees to sign contracts or waivers prohibiting disclosure of their wages and expands retaliation protections to workers who inquire about, discuss, or disclose wages [S2] [S3].
The EEOC must collect annual compensation data disaggregated by sex, race, and national origin from employers with 100 or more employees, for use in investigating pay discrimination charges [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, particularly larger ones. They face expanded lawsuit exposure with new damages categories, new administrative duties (pay data reporting, workplace notices), and in some cases will have to restructure pay practices that currently produce gaps. Small businesses that are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act are exempt here too [S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers would face significantly higher litigation risk, since narrowed defenses, punitive damages, and class actions raise the cost of even good-faith pay practices that fall short, and businesses bear new compliance and reporting burdens [S3].
The measure exempts small enterprises to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, so many small employers and their employees fall outside its protections [S3].
Training, research, and grant programs in the bill are funded by 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate attached, an open-ended federal authorization [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing sex-based pay gaps, the bill materially changes the balance: today the employer controls the evidence and the legal standard is easy to meet; the bill shifts the burden, adds damages, and bars salary-history practices that import past discrimination into new jobs. The main cost falls on employers in the form of compliance work and litigation exposure, which is the intended deterrent, though opponents argue it invites lawsuits over legitimate pay differences. The small-business exemption limits both the benefit and the burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Workforce and Oversight committees on introduction day, never got a committee vote or floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 10, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and the Committee on Oversight and Accountability [S5].
The bill accumulated 221 cosponsors, 220 House Democrats and 1 House Republican, but no further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they keep the current legal standard, under which they need only show any factor other than sex explains a pay gap, and they avoid new pay-data reporting and expanded damages. House Republicans who opposed the measure also benefit, since a vote would have forced members to go on record.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro

for.name: 220 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it near-unanimous support within the caucus.

against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee, the bill's primary referral, never held a markup or vote on it in two years.

against.name: James Comer
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Accountability Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the bill's second referral, never took action on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 220 Democratic cosponsors joined against a single Republican; the committees and leadership that never moved the bill were both controlled by Republicans, so the split fell almost entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The bill narrows their legal defense against equal pay claims, adds compensatory and punitive damages and class actions, bans salary-history questions, and requires annual pay data reporting by sex, race, and national origin. The cost is compliance and litigation exposure; the benefit to workers is stronger enforcement of equal pay.

Small enterprises are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, so most of the bill's duties and liabilities skip them, though their employees also get no new protections.

industries.industry: Human resources and payroll compliance services
industries.note: Annual compensation-data reporting by 100+ employee employers and new workplace notice requirements would create compliance work for data, payroll, and HR services firms.
